## Interbranch Representation {background-image="https://www.byrdcenter.org/uploads/6/7/8/7/67873389/403958_orig.jpg?592" background-opacity=".2"}

- Constituency service/casework
  - residents 
  - nonprofits, businesses, state & local governments <!-- identity groups --> 
- Policy work 
  - oversight 
  - advocacy in agency policymaking

$\approx$ all substantive representation to another branch

<!--
For Congress, $\approx$ all representation not through legislating

<!--- Ellie (9/1): I'm commenting out the all representation not through legislation. I think that gets us in trouble with the speech as representation folks. No need to pick that battle. Need to cut space anyway. 
--> 

::: {.notes}
Today I'm going to talk about a book I'm writing on interbranch representation, which includes a bunch of things that have been studied separately.

Part of the argument of the book is that there is this set of things that we treat as separate, but are actually linked in multiple ways such that it makes sense to study them as a whole. 
(1) they are done by the same staff
(2) they are received and processed in the same systems by agencies
(3) they feed into one another, new policy creates new casework, new casework is the fodder of new policy
:::

## Today 

1. Situate the book project 
2. Preview findings & policy implications
3. Theory: A unified framework
4. New data: 840,000 congressional requests to 100+ agencies
5. Design: cross-sectional & two-way fixed effect models of year-legislator-agency counts
6. Findings

## The book

What drives variation in interbranch work? 

```{r}
#| label: fig-percent
#| fig-cap: "Observed levels of interbranch representation per legislator per year"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Senate"
#|   - "House"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 95%

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "percentile-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "percentile-2.png"))
```

::: {.notes}
This matters because there is huge inequality in interbranch representation.

Here we have the average number of requests each legislator makes to federal agencies on the y-axis, organized by their percentile in the distribution in their chamber. 

 The top decile in both the Senate and House is doing 5 x the amount that the median legislator does. And 10 x the lower quartile.

You've probably heard of Gini Coefficients as a measure of inequality being used to describe income inequality. 
Top 10 most unequal countries, including Honduras at .47 and Zimbabwe at .50

AND THIS IS TRUE FOR ALL OF THE TYPES OF REPRESENTATION WE LOOK AT
- constituency casework on behalf of individuals 
- on behalf of businesses
- on behalf of nonprofits and local governments 
- also true for policy work 

So this is what we want to explain --- how we are doing this. 
:::

## Puzzle: Why do some offices do so much more interbranch work? 

. . . 

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Senator Byrd's Office](byrdoffice.jpg)
Senator Byrd's Office
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](cruzoffice.jpg)
Senator Cruz's Office
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The story we are telling is not just about legislators, but CONGRESSIONAL OFFICES and what they are organized to do --- they are not the same. We often study legislators as politicians, but we think it is important to also study congressional offices as bureaucracies. 

Senator Byrd's office here on the right looks like a place where you might write some letters on letterhead.
Senator Cruz office looks more like a podcasting studio. His style of representation is not what some call the workhorse style. 

And indeed, Byrd is at the top of that graph I just showed you, and
Cruz is at the very bottom

:::

##

### What drives variation in interbranch work? 

. . . 

`Demand`: More and more demanding constituents

`Capacity`: Big legislator experience & staffing effects. Committee staff increase policy work (even of non-chairs)

`Strategic incentives` shape some types of representation

- Little relationship with **electoral** incentives 
- Strong **partisan/ideological** effects; mostly working with executive-branch *allies*, except on behalf of business
- Committee work extends *preexisting* **policy interests**

<hr>

Positively correlated with legislating and fundraising.

## Policy implications 

**Term limits** would likely have unappreciated costs.

**More staff**^[Not communications staff] would increase constituency service and rebalance power (e.g., New Deal, Nixon).

<!-- The president commands 10,000x more FTE than the highest-capacity legislator, 100x more than Congress
- Given more staff, offices mostly do things people like--> 

**Centralizing executive power** likely reduces congressional oversight, representation, and influence in policymaking and implementation.

**Shared congressional & agency infrastructure** opportunities.

**Campaign finance reform** may matter after all. 

::: {.notes}
The president commands 10,000x more FTE than the highest-capacity legislator, 100x more than Congress.
:::

## What we know {.smaller}

Members of Congress contact agencies to represent: 

- constituents' needs [@Fiorina1977; @Fenno1978; @MillsKalafHughes2015; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @SnyderJudgeLordPowellGrimmer2025]
- constituents' policy preferences [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023]
- shared identity groups [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019]
- corporate donors [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]
<!-- the institution of congress [@USDepartmentofJustice2016] -->

This varies by 

- institutional position [@Lowande2018APSR; @LowandePotter2021; @LauterbachRitchie2025; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026]
- experience [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @Lowande2018APSR; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026] & effectiveness [@KalafHughes2023]
- party status [@Lowande2019; @Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @LauterbachRitchie2025]
- partisan/ideological alignment [@Lowande2019; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @Lowande2018APSR;  @LauterbachRitchie2025]

Maybe also electoral competition [@Fiorina1977; @Rivers1989; @King1991], but maybe not [@Ritchie2023]

::: {.notes}
When we started this project, it was old work by Fenno and Fiorina, and a cool new paper that Russ Mills and Nicky Kalaf-Hughes presented 10 years ago at MPSA. Since then, we've learned a number of things. 
To sum up all of this very briefly
[READ SLIDE VERY FAST]
So we have good evidence that all of these factors (except elections) matter on the margins. 
This paper aims to build on and scaffold around this work. 
:::

## What we don't know 

Existing studies: 

- Examine **one or a small number of agencies**. What does it look like across all agencies? 
- Focus on a **single type of interbranch representation**. What is the broader picture? 
- Unclear how it all fits together


::: {.notes}
This paper aims to build on and scaffold around this work. 

We fill in some gaps, [READ SLIDE]
:::

## A unified framework 


```{r}
#| label: fig-causal
#| fig-cap: "Constituent demand, capacity, and strategic incentives"
#| out-width: "100%"

#TODO get the updated version 
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "mermaid-figure-1.png"))
```


::: {.notes}
We organize explanations into three broad possible causes of variation that likely drive different kinds of representation. Then we ask big-picture questions about how important each cause is in aggregate for different outcomes.
:::


## A unified framework

Demand

- more `constituents`, more `needy` or `demanding` constituents

Capacity

- more `staff`, `expertise`, etc. 

Strategic incentives to do more in certain contexts

- `reelection`, `partisan/ideological`, `institutional` incentives

<hr>

1. Who is represented? (e.g., individuals, businesses, etc.)
2. What kind of work? (e.g., casework, policy work)

<!--also reflect **distribution** of interests--> 

::: {.notes}
This 3-part organization is similar to how Ritchie has organized these causes, 
except perhaps that we put oversight more in the "strategic incentives" bucket, as Lowande's 2018 paper does.
Though it is probably both, the fact that we see members paying special attention to agencies in advance of joining that agency's oversight committee makes us think that Strategic Incentives is a relatively better interpretation of the oversight committee's effects.  
[READ SLIDE]


In this paper, we try to put almost all of these together. We have not yet incorporated measures of having more demanding (for example, higher-income) constituents.

We are also not focusing on predictors of allocation across agencies. That was the topic of our last year's MPSA papers. 

In this paper, we ask how much each of these factors drives variation in how much interbranch representation different districts receive. 

We can think about representation varying along two dimensions: (1) WHO someone is representing and (2) WHAT kind of action the representative is taking to do so. 

[Read slide] 
:::

## Data  {.incremental}

~400,000 legislator-agency-year counts (840,000 legislator requests to 100+ agencies, 2000-2024) 

. . . 

\+ District demographics [@tidycensus]

\+ Legislator experience in office, prior office [@VoldenWiseman2014]

\+ Staff experience and allocation [@congressional_staff; @CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021]

\+ Committee positions & jurisdiction [@committees; @LewisSelin2012]

\+ Electoral competitiveness [@Thomsen2023], legislator ideology (voting-based) [@dwnominate2024], perceived agency ideology (survey-based) [@RichardsonClintonLewis2018]


::: {.notes}
We now have data from over 100 agencies from 2000-2024, including all departments except for the Department of State. It has now been 9 years since I filed that request. To be fair, State originally told us it would take 6 years, so they are only 3 years behind schedule. 

This has taken a ton of work, negotiation, threatening lawsuits, and data cleaning, which I will not go into for the sake of time. 

We tally up the number of requests per legislator, per agency, per year, 
yielding legislator-agency-year observations

These are counts, so fit a negative binomial count model, with indicators for 
demand, like the number of people in the state  
capacity, like committee chair positions and years in office, and 
Strategic Incentives, like oversight committee membership, majority party status, whether you have a co-partisan presidential electoral vulnerability, and 
ideological distance from the agency, which we get by subtracting nominee scores from Richardson-Clinton-Lewis scores. 
and other things
Errors are clustered at the legislator level. 
:::

## Design {.not-scrollable}


Two-way fixed effects 

$$ 
\tiny
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt}\mid X_{ijt},\delta_{jt}, \gamma_{ij}  
 & \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_{ijt},\alpha), \\
\log(\mu_{ijt}) = 
 & \beta_1 \text{District Population}_{it} + \beta_2 \text{Experience in Office}_{it}+ \\
 & \beta_3 \text{Committee Leadership Position}_{it} + \beta_4 \text{Oversight Committee Position}_{ijt}+ \\
 & \beta_5 \text{Majority Party}_{it} + \beta_6 \text{President's Party}_{it} + \\
 & \beta_7 \text{Competitive General Election}_{it} + \beta_8 \text{Competitive Primary Election}_{it} + \\
 & \beta_9 \text{Perceived Ideological Distance from Agency}_{ijt} + \\
 & ... + \delta_{jt} + \gamma_{ij} \\
 & \text{Errors clustered at the legislator level.}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-diff1}




## Design {.not-scrollable}


$Y_{ijt}$ = requests legislator $i$ makes to agency $j$ in year $t$

. . . 

$\delta_{jt}$ is an **agency--year** fixed effect

. . . 

$\gamma_{ij}$ **legislator--agency** fixed effect

- time-invariant legislator characteristics
- legislator--agency factors, including stable state or district attributes (population, demographics, local industries) that shape demand.

::: {.notes}
Important here are fixed effects for agency-year pairs, which cover shocks to agencies like scandals and censoring in our data 
in all models 
We also estimate difference-in-differences with fixed effects for the legislator-agency pair, so those models are just about within-legislator variation over time. 

I'm happy to click over to the regression table slides in Q&A, but 
We have a large sample, so we get to focus on the magnitude of effects. 
:::

::: {.notes}
So I'm going to show you a bunch of average marginal effects, in percentage terms. 

The average percentage difference in legislator requests per year is on the Y-axis.

This first compares a one SD change in state population and, by implication, equal staff budgets for Senators. 

Each point estimate is the percentage change for a different type of interbranch representation. 

Population thus represents both demand and capacity and explains a large share of variation in the Senate, but not all of it: about 20% of the overall inequality in interbranch representation in the Senate.

::: {.notes}
There is a causal effect of joining a committee, but it is smaller than the cross-sectional effect. One interpretation here is that members have preexisting interests that lead them to join committees with jurisdiction over those agencies. (e.g., I'm from an ag-heavy state; I join the Ag committee), but then they do more --- the within-legislator design shows members increasing policy work with an agency when they join a committee overseeing that agency. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: results-matrix

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

type_levels <- c("Const. Service", "Corp. Service",  "NGO/Gov't Service", "Corp. Policy", "General Policy", "Total") 

element_levels <- c("Demand", "Capacity", "Strategic incentives")

sub_elements <- tribble(
  ~element,               ~sub,
  "Demand",               "Number of constituents",
  "Demand",               "Neediness of constituents",
  "Demand",               "Political savvy of constituents",
  "Capacity",             "Senate",
  "Capacity",             "Experience in Congress",
  "Capacity",             "Experience in state leg.",
  "Capacity",             "Committee leadership",
  "Capacity",             "Reporting committee seat",
  "Capacity",             "Staff volume",
  "Capacity",             "Staff allocation",
  "Strategic incentives", "Partisan alignment",
  "Strategic incentives", "Ideological alignment",
  "Strategic incentives", "Business",
  "Strategic incentives", "Electoral incentives",
  "Strategic incentives", "Institutional incentives"
)

library(readr)
results <- read_csv(here::here("tables/sub_elements.csv") ) |> group_by(element, sub) |> 
  pivot_longer(#!element, !sub,
    #cols = c(element, sub),
               cols = c(
    "Const. Service",
    "Corp. Service",
    "NGO/Gov't Service",
    "General Policy",
    "Corp. Policy",
    "Total"),
    names_to = "outcome",
    values_to = "support")
# Build the full grid, then fill in your actual codings.

results2 <- results |>
  mutate(
    #outcome = gsub("\\n", "\n", outcome, fixed = TRUE),
    element = factor(element, levels = element_levels),
    sub     = factor(sub, levels = rev(sub_elements$sub)),
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = type_levels),
    support = factor(support, levels = c("Strong", "Mixed", "None"))
  )

ggplot(results2, aes(x = outcome, y = sub)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 5.5, xmax = 6.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey92", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = support), shape = 21, size = 6, stroke = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    Strong = "#009E73",
    Mixed  = "#F0E442",
    None   = "white"
  )) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  facet_grid(element ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Strong = expected direction, significant across most measures;\nMixed = significant in some measures; None = no support.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x.top = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, lineheight = 0.9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, angle = 0, hjust = 1),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.y = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40", hjust = 0)
  )
```


## To sum up: 

`Demand` matters, but is far from the full story.

`Capacity`: Big legislator experience & staffing effects. Committee staff increase policy work (even of non-chairs)

`Strategic incentives` shape some types of representation

- Little relationship with **electoral** incentives 
- Strong **partisan/ideological** patterns; mostly working with *allied agencies*, except on behalf of business
- Committee positions further *preexisting* **policy interests**

Positively correlated with legislating and fundraising.

Interbranch infrastructure is a mess.

## Why so unequal? {visibility="uncounted"}

Demand & capacity

- Senators representing more people with more staff 
- Unequal access to committee staff 
- Unequal experience
- Unequal allocations of staff to interbranch work

Strategic Incentives explain attention allocation and volume, but not inequality.

- Effects spread across high and low performers $\rightarrow$ no impact on inequality 


::: {.notes}

:::


## Design (Dirichlet) {visibility="uncounted"}


$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Y}_i \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i),
\qquad
\alpha_{ij} = \phi_i \mu_{ij},
\end{equation}
$$

$$
\begin{equation}
\log\left(\frac{\mu_{ij}}{\mu_{iK}}\right)
=
\beta_{0j} + \sum_{p=1}^{P}\beta_{pj}x_{ip},
\qquad j=1,\ldots,K-1.
\end{equation}
$$





::: {.notes}
Important here are
fixed effects for agency-year pairs, which cover shocks to agencies like scandals and censoring in our data 
in all models 
We also estimate difference-in-differences with fixed effects for the legislator-agency pair, so those models are just about within-legislator variation over time. 

I'm happy to click over to the regression table slides in Q&A, but 
We have a large sample, so we get to focus on the magnitude of effects. 
:::
